summary: Morgan Tsvangirai founded the Movement for Democratic Change, launched in January.

MDC president Morgan Tsvangirai says the party is considering a national strike, international sanctions, and a possible boycott of coming parliamentary elections to protest state-sponsored violence against its members.

Morgan Tsvangirai, the opposition leader, accepted that the rural vote in Zimbabwe's elections reflected rural people's views and acknowledged that the opposition Movement for Democratic Change had insufficient access to rural areas.

Zimbabwe's defeated opposition party, the Movement for Democratic Change, plans to take 10 dossiers listing alleged election rigging to the high court, covering events including the defeat of MDC leader Morgan Tsvangirai in Buhera North.

Zimbabwean high court postponed opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai's terrorism trial while the supreme court considers the constitutionality of the colonial-era Law and Order (Maintenance) Act used to charge him.

Morgan Tsvangirai faces scrutiny over a videotaped meeting with a lobbying firm in which he did not object to statements about assassinating President Robert Mugabe, ahead of Zimbabwe's presidential election.

Morgan Tsvangirai's Movement for Democratic Change prepares to argue in court that Robert Mugabe won Zimbabwe's presidential election through massive fraud and violence.

Zimbabwean police question Morgan Tsvangirai for several hours and say they plan to charge him with threatening President Robert Mugabe under new security laws.

A court in Zimbabwe orders opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai to be released on bail after two weeks of detention on treason charges, with restrictions on his political statements.

Morgan Tsvangirai, leader of Zimbabwe's opposition Movement for Democratic Change, was acquitted of treason charges.

Morgan Tsvangirai urged South Africa and neighboring countries to press President Robert Mugabe to meet minimum standards for free and fair elections, saying his party had not yet decided whether to participate in March parliamentary elections.

Morgan Tsvangirai decides to pull out of Friday's presidential run-off in Zimbabwe.

Zimbabwean opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai and two aides had their passports confiscated at the airport as they tried to fly to South Africa for a summit, though the passports were later returned.

Morgan Tsvangirai is introduced as Zimbabwe's prime minister at a power-sharing signing ceremony, calling the agreement a product of a painful compromise.

Morgan Tsvangirai, sworn in as Zimbabwe's prime minister earlier in February 2009, faces resistance from Robert Mugabe and Zanu-PF, who are undermining the unity government and limiting his control.

Morgan Tsvangirai left hospital a day after surviving a car crash that killed his wife, Susan.

Morgan Tsvangirai said there was no going back on the unity government he formed with President Robert Mugabe.
Morgan Tsvangirai said his efforts to restore democratic freedoms and the rule of law in Zimbabwe had so far failed, citing frustration from hard-liners backing Robert Mugabe.

Morgan Tsvangirai, prime minister of Zimbabwe, discusses his power-sharing agreement with President Robert Mugabe, describing their meetings as cordial and expressing belief that Mugabe is committed to the unity government.
